User-approved ontology fact (2026-11-21): Organ is a complete high-level logical Agent in HumanAgent, with its own logical identity, capability boundary, lifecycle, execution responsibility, and recovery responsibility. It is not an alias for a runtime, provider session, process, UI, or a specific execution product.

Identity: OrganId identifies the high-level logical Agent only. It is not a DSH/ACP/OpenCode session id, runtime id, process PID, provider identity, or UI instance id.

Cardinality and runtime: an Organ type may be singleton or group. The explicit Brain has exactly one Organ and one runtime instance. The implicit Brain and other Agents may have multiple runtime instances. Runtime instances are replaceable execution carriers and never replace Organ identity.

Execution backend: DSH, ACP, OpenCode, and future backends bind through the execution-runtime contract/adapter boundary. Backend types and session identities must not be promoted into the Organ domain type. Current MVP delivery still uses the fake backend and must not claim real DSH/ACP/OpenCode adapter completion from this architecture fact.

UI relation: an Organ may have UI or have no UI. UI is decoupled from Organ. UI is not part of Organ identity and never owns Organ lifecycle. When UI exists, it observes or controls Organ only through typed projection and command ports. Without UI, Organ must still be independently creatable, runnable, recoverable, stoppable, and observable through legal observation ports. UI must not directly read Journal, provider sessions, runtime internals, or raw health-probe output.

Owners: Organ identity/lifecycle/error/recovery semantics are owned by packages/core; runtime instances, admission, scheduling, checkpoint orchestration, and recovery flow by packages/runtime; external backend adaptation by the corresponding adapters; UI projection/command/product shell by packages/ui; assembly by packages/app.

content:
User-approved ontology fact v3 (2026-11-21): Task is a user-visible, persistent business work object with a stable TaskId, Goal, Goal revision, state machine, Notebook, and owning Organ. A Task is not a subagent short exploration.

Task kind has exactly two top-level types: one-shot and periodic. A one-shot Task has one final completion point and may still span many Cycles. A periodic Task has a wakeup mechanism and repeatedly creates Occurrences. The current long-running concept is not a third top-level type; maintenance work such as manager board patrol, agent scheduling, problem handling, and resource recovery is a periodic profile. Periodic profiles may include inspection, maintenance, and generic-recurring. Periodic Tasks may wake or run concurrently with other periodic Tasks.

Task triggers are not limited to direct user input. A Task trigger may come from user input, scheduler wakeup, another Task event, an Organ or manager event, a system error/health/resource event, or an external event. Each trigger follows the same intake path: receive trigger, load context, decide whether to create a new Task, update an existing Task Goal, or only record an event. An error found during patrol may create a remediation Task only when task-creation policy or rules determine that the finding needs an independently tracked business work item; observations do not automatically become Tasks.

Task state machine is deliberately reduced to four main states: created, active, waiting, and closed. created means the Task is registered but its initial Goal, admission, or confirmation is incomplete. active means the Task remains valid and can progress; queued, running, evaluating, settling, and recovering are execution details owned by Cycle, Operation, or Checkpoint rather than Task main states. waiting means the Task cannot progress now but remains recoverable, with a waitReason such as admission, user-input, goal-confirmation, dependency, resource, error-recovery, blocked, or next-occurrence. closed means the Task no longer executes, with an outcome of succeeded, failed, cancelled, or stopped.

Legal main-state transitions are: created to active, waiting, or closed; active to active, waiting, or closed; waiting to active or closed; closed has no outgoing transition. Recoverable error is Task waiting with waitReason error-recovery and retained recovery responsibility; unrecoverable error is closed with outcome failed. Journal-read uncertainty is represented separately by recoveryStatus and is not a normal business state.

Goal update behavior applies to any trigger that can change an existing Task. The order is fixed: assess trigger against current Goal and context; if update is required, trigger Goal update; commit new Goal revision; reassess next execution using the new revision; then choose the Task state transition and execution path. Execution must not continue a new Goal with an old Goal revision. Prompt text, model output, or logs must not replace the Journal-committed Goal revision. User-approved ontology fact (2026-11-21): Organ is a complete high-level logical Agent in HumanAgent, with its own logical identity, capability boundary, lifecycle, execution responsibility, and recovery responsibility. It is not an alias for a runtime, provider session, process, UI, or a specific execution product.

Identity: OrganId identifies the high-level logical Agent only. It is not a DSH/ACP/OpenCode session id, runtime id, process PID, provider identity, or UI instance id.

Cardinality and runtime: an Organ type may be singleton or group. The explicit Brain has exactly one Organ and one runtime instance. The implicit Brain and other Agents may have multiple runtime instances. Runtime instances are replaceable execution carriers and never replace Organ identity.

Execution backend: DSH, ACP, OpenCode, and future backends bind through the execution-runtime contract/adapter boundary. Backend types and session identities must not be promoted into the Organ domain type. Current MVP delivery still uses the fake backend and must not claim real DSH/ACP/OpenCode adapter completion from this architecture fact.

UI relation: an Organ may have UI or have no UI. UI is decoupled from Organ. UI is not part of Organ identity and never owns Organ lifecycle. When UI exists, it observes or controls Organ only through typed projection and command ports. Without UI, Organ must still be independently creatable, runnable, recoverable, stoppable, and observable through legal observation ports. UI must not directly read Journal, provider sessions, runtime internals, or raw health-probe output.

Owners: Organ identity/lifecycle/error/recovery semantics are owned by packages/core; runtime instances, admission, scheduling, checkpoint orchestration, and recovery flow by packages/runtime; external backend adaptation by the corresponding adapters; UI projection/command/product shell by packages/ui; assembly by packages/app.

content:
User-approved ontology fact v3 (2026-11-21): Task is a user-visible, persistent business work object with a stable TaskId, Goal, Goal revision, state machine, Notebook, and owning Organ. A Task is not a subagent short exploration.

Task kind has exactly two top-level types: one-shot and periodic. A one-shot Task has one final completion point and may still span many Cycles. A periodic Task has a wakeup mechanism and repeatedly creates Occurrences. The current long-running concept is not a third top-level type; maintenance work such as manager board patrol, agent scheduling, problem handling, and resource recovery is a periodic profile. Periodic profiles may include inspection, maintenance, and generic-recurring. Periodic Tasks may wake or run concurrently with other periodic Tasks.

Task triggers are not limited to direct user input. A Task trigger may come from user input, scheduler wakeup, another Task event, an Organ or manager event, a system error/health/resource event, or an external event. Each trigger follows the same intake path: receive trigger, load context, decide whether to create a new Task, update an existing Task Goal, or only record an event. An error found during patrol may create a remediation Task only when task-creation policy or rules determine that the finding needs an independently tracked business work item; observations do not automatically become Tasks.

Task state machine is deliberately reduced to four main states: created, active, waiting, and closed. created means the Task is registered but its initial Goal, admission, or confirmation is incomplete. active means the Task remains valid and can progress; queued, running, evaluating, settling, and recovering are execution details owned by Cycle, Operation, or Checkpoint rather than Task main states. waiting means the Task cannot progress now but remains recoverable, with a waitReason such as admission, user-input, goal-confirmation, dependency, resource, error-recovery, blocked, or next-occurrence. closed means the Task no longer executes, with an outcome of succeeded, failed, cancelled, or stopped.

Legal main-state transitions are: created to active, waiting, or closed; active to active, waiting, or closed; waiting to active or closed; closed has no outgoing transition. Recoverable error is Task waiting with waitReason error-recovery and retained recovery responsibility; unrecoverable error is closed with outcome failed. Journal-read uncertainty is represented separately by recoveryStatus and is not a normal business state.

Goal update behavior applies to any trigger that can change an existing Task. The order is fixed: assess trigger against current Goal and context; if update is required, trigger Goal update; commit new Goal revision; reassess next execution using the new revision; then choose the Task state transition and execution path. Execution must not continue a new Goal with an old Goal revision. Prompt text, model output, or logs must not replace the Journal-committed Goal revision. New Task creation commits the initial Goal revision; that is initial creation, not a Goal update.

The Task update flow is modeled as a SESE DAG per trigger: receive Task Trigger; parse source and context; branch between create Task and process existing Task; create path commits the initial Goal revision; existing path assesses Goal update and, when required, commits the new revision; all paths converge to reassess execution, select active/waiting/closed, commit state and control result, record event/checkpoint/receipt, and close the trigger handling at a single exit. Retries, confirmations, periodic wakeups, and recovery are new DAG executions and are not static back edges.

Relations: a Task belongs to one owning Organ and has many Goal revisions, TaskPlan revisions, Cycles, Assignments, PlanSteps, and Operations. A periodic Task has many Occurrences. Each Task has one Task Notebook that records progress, decisions, blockers, evidence, and next steps by Cycle. Notebook and checkpoint are not lifecycle truth. The Organ Journal owns Task state, Goal revision, checkpoint, and control-event truth. Subagent explorations remain Assignment, PlanStep, Cycle, or Operation inside the parent Task and do not become user-level Tasks.

Implementation gap versus current code: packages/contracts currently exposes one-shot/inspection/long-running as one TaskFlowKind layer and reuses LifecycleState across Task, Cycle, Operation, and Pipeline Node; core/runtime still lack the Task-specific four-state machine, unified TaskTrigger, trigger-to-create/update policy, and SESE state-update graph. Existing updateTask directly edits directive and increments revision instead of applying assess, Goal update, revision commit, execution reassessment, and state transition. Periodic scheduler, Occurrence, and Notebook runtime capabilities remain MVP gaps; an in-execution sleep must not be presented as background periodic wakeup.
title: Ontology: Task is a trigger-driven business work object

content:
User-approved ontology fact (2026-11-21): Goal is the persistent semantic target of one Task. It answers what must be achieved, within which scope, under which business rules, and against which acceptance criteria. Goal is not a Task, execution plan, prompt, runtime state, provider goal object, Notebook, or scheduler.

A Task has one logical Goal. The Goal has immutable GoalRevision snapshots and one current accepted revision. A GoalRevision contains the complete target snapshot, including objective, scope, acceptance criteria, business rules, predecessor identity, source trigger, confirmation reference, and authoritative journal commit reference. Only a Journal-committed revision is control truth. A draft, model suggestion, prompt string, Notebook entry, provider tool state, or log cannot become Goal truth.

GoalRevision changes only when target content changes: objective, scope, acceptance criteria, or business rules. It must not change for wakeup timing, busy state, scheduler lease, execution epoch, provider/runtime selection, retry, settling, or recovery. Scheduling or dispatch-control changes use a separate DispatchPolicyRevision chain. A periodic Task receives the standard dispatch semantics from its TaskKind/periodic profile rather than embedding wakeup fields in Goal.

Goal status is deliberately small: active or retired. active means the Goal remains effective and may drive plans and Cycles. retired means the Goal no longer drives execution. Task waiting, blocked, error recovery, next-occurrence waiting, and final outcome belong to Task state, waitReason, outcome, Cycle, or Operation state; they do not become Goal states. A Task closure retires its Goal, but completion/cancellation/failure outcomes are owned by Task.

Goal update order is fixed for any legal trigger: receive trigger; read the current GoalRevision; assess whether target content must change; if update is required, pass the confirmation gate; generate the Goal proposal; commit the new GoalRevision; make it the current revision; then reassess execution and choose the Task state/action. Existing Task target, scope, or handling changes still require separate confirmation. If confirmation is pending or rejected, the current GoalRevision stays unchanged. Prompt/model output cannot overwrite Goal, and execution cannot continue a changed target with an old revision.

New Task creation creates the initial Goal revision; that is initial creation, not a Goal update. An event that creates a remediation Task creates a new Task and new Goal rather than mutating the source Task Goal.

Periodic wakeup is standard dispatch behavior, not Goal content. When a periodic wakeup is due, the control owner reads the current GoalRevision and atomically checks busy state while claiming execution ownership. Busy handling follows the Task's dispatch policy. Under `busyPolicy=skip`, a busy wakeup commits a skipped-busy receipt, starts no concurrent Cycle, and closes that wakeup. Under the patrol `idle-reminder` policy, the whole cycle defers while busy; when the executor becomes idle, the pending reminder wakes it immediately and the original cadence resumes from that actual reminder time. If busy is false, the normal path creates an Occurrence, creates or allocates a Cycle, binds that Cycle to the current GoalRevision, and dispatches the owning Agent. Busy must be decided from active execution control facts such as an active Cycle, un-settled Operation, valid Occurrence claim, or valid execution lease, in one atomic check-and-claim operation. Notebook, model output, provider logs, and UI snapshots are not busy control truth.

If a GoalRevision commits before a wakeup claim, that wakeup uses the new revision. When the user confirms a Goal change during execution, the Task immediately enters the Goal-change flow and the current Cycle stops advancing the old Goal. Clarify the new requirement and commit the updated Goal. Compare existing results with its acceptance criteria, update the plan from the remaining gap, and continue the same Task under the updated Goal. Work already performed retains the GoalRevision under which it ran.

Relations: Task 1--1 Goal; Goal 1--* GoalRevision; TaskPlanRevision must reference the GoalRevision it was planned from; Goal 1--0..* Subscription/Occurrence through the periodic Task dispatch policy; Occurrence 1--1 Cycle when execution starts; Wakeup 1--0..1 Cycle because a skipped-busy wakeup produces no Cycle and an idle-reminder wakeup defers Cycle creation until it is sent. Goal update handling and standard periodic wakeup handling are separate SESE DAGs. Each new trigger or due wakeup re-enters its DAG; retry, confirmation, and the next period do not create static back edges.

Current implementation gap: packages/contracts GoalRecord is only a small record and exposes active/completed/cancelled/suspended, mixing Goal and Task outcome states. Existing Subscription/Occurrence/Reminder/lease contracts already model dispatch control and must stay outside Goal content. The runtime lacks a committed GoalRevision chain, an explicit TaskPlanRevision-to-GoalRevision binding, atomic busy check-and-claim wakeup semantics, and a Goal projection separate from directive text. updateTask still mutates directive/directiveRevision directly instead of applying assess, confirm, commit GoalRevision, and reassess execution. Provider tool goal state is a temporary runtime artifact, not domain Goal truth. No product implementation is claimed by this approved ontology fact.
title: Ontology: Goal carries target semantics, not dispatch control
